speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is scope to enhance our procurement practices towards promoting innovation among our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) while, at the same time, delivering value for money for the public sector.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could be a new category of tenders carved out for projects where the public sector agencies intend to co-create solutions with SMEs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In such tenders, the procurement of innovations is better achieved by specifying the public sector problems to be solved rather than by prescribing the solution and the work to be done, which is the usual approach.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to allow for sufficient discretion at the operating level for bite-size public sector projects to be awarded to small businesses which may be early movers or who are proactive in coming up with innovative solutions that the public agencies are looking for.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Subjecting every proposal to an open tender would be the surest way to kill off initiative and creativity among the small businesses, and some could be start-ups.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Understandably, there is a need to devise new and alternative governance safeguards other than just making every tenderer compete on prices in the name of transparency and fairness.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Getting the best price tender may not necessarily bring out the most creative and innovative solution which serve the long-term needs of the public sector.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The cumulative solution may not be a more sustainable solution.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the private sector, awarding contracts on the basis of ideas and innovation by large companies to small firms are already prevalent.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many developed countries' public sectors do have tailor-made procurement practices too that promote innovations and co-creations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can take a leaf from the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To help SMEs develop innovative solutions to public sector challenges, the UK government established the Small Business Research Initiative (SBRI) specifically to help small companies compete for government projects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SBRI helps to connect small businesses to government departments which have public sector problems and assist small businesses come up with innovative solutions and ideas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This scheme even helps with bridge financing and, in cases of new invention, to safeguard the intellectual property.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Singapore, we do have a similar scheme known as Public-Private Co-Innovation Partnership (CI Partnership), which is the platform for Government departments and local companies to co-develop innovative solutions to meet the Government's needs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, upon deeper study into the details on the CI Partnership website, it seems that this scheme has turned dormant.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of the criteria mentioned was that during the commercialisation phase, the agency may need to call for an open tender to procure the innovative product or service.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But now, with greater emphasis on working closely with businesses and to foster innovation, the Government should give this scheme another boost and fine tune the criteria and KPIs to be more innovation friendly.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What can the Government do to help smaller firms better access Government procurement opportunities and to build a track record for their overseas expansion?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cumbersome procurement processes and irrelevant qualifying criteria, such as how big the company is and the number of years in operation, have deterred many SMEs, especially the start-ups, from supplying solutions to the Government where innovative and creative procurement is concerned.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should introduce greater flexibilities in the way the Government sector procures goods and services, including looking at non-traditional safeguards to ensure value for money.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Developing a more SME-friendly procurement process will allow SMEs the opportunities to harness their creativity and capabilities, yet result in higher competition on ideas and solutions, leading to better value for money for the public sector agencies.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Escalation clauses need not be used only to protect the contractors when the costs go up.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: They can also be used to favour the Government when key costs drop, say, commodity or oil prices.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: They can provide that in such cases, the contract price to be paid by the Government will decrease accordingly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: After 50 years of good progress, it is timely for us, as a nation, to reflect and begin charting new directions together to scale new heights for the next 50 years and more.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As the Minister for Finance calls for better partnership with industry and our people, what areas can we look at to co-create solutions?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Here are some areas that may be worth considering.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With many sectors in the broad-based industry, each sector has its unique characteristics and needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To enhance and find areas of synergy, it is pertinent for the different sectors to provide insights and champion ideas that they believe would put our industries on a better footing on the global stage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Ministry should provide platforms for such collective ideas to take shape.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Each sector should allow natural champions in leading their own industry to define the framework and seek support in areas of assistance required to differentiate themselves as a business or as a Singapore brand.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For community leaders, we need flexibility in defining guidelines and, during its implementation, to encourage co-ownership and innovation with local adaptation of ground-up initiatives to suit their needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is a culture that we seek to foster with both our industries and our people.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Reduce top-down directive that is, in return, strengthened by our social recognition of what we define together as a community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Next, to create enhanced support with a planned roadmap for these outfits.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Take, for example, our social enterprises that have emerged over the years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many have embarked on the path due to their passion and belief to support specific causes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, many have closed down over time from an inability to sustain due to funding or other reasons.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This way, it allows the enterprises to harness resources and leverage capabilities to sustain or learn best practices.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Lastly, in all solutions initiated, it is critical to have a closed loop to improve the feedback channel and finetune the system instead of adding more features continuously which, invariably, result in some complexity and redundancies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Before we move full swing to introduce services, there are a few aspects that are necessary to be deliberated.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, sufficient effort must be made for different groups of participants, be they businesses, citizens, voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) and so on, to understand the significance and tangible benefits of such implementation rather than viewing the process as yet another target.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The initial process may be long, but these efforts are necessary, without which, any momentum in the transformation would be painfully slow and is likely to achieve a lower success rate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It may also cost us more since additional resources have to be injected at a later stage because it is more of a "push" than a "pull" process.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Assurance is also necessary that the push for such electronic service delivery within Government agencies does not result in lesser clarity of ownership on the issues or become a revolving door.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As it stands, many organisations already have different forms of operating systems and databases that they use to handle the operational tasks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, the regular audit process still requires massive amounts of manual backend paperwork, filing and keeping of records in order for all these audits to take place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The question remains if the methods of handling audits are contradictory to the digitalisation efforts, while remaining a necessary and critical check of any organisation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Time and cost on both parties would be alleviated when fewer processes are reinvented and streamlined.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And of course, the most critical link is the need for inclusiveness when systems and processes are designed because the ability of the different groups to adapt will vary in society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Care-givers are becoming a vulnerable group themselves while they care for their vulnerable loved ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They face emotional stress, lack of social support and immediate and long-term financial burdens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is worse for specialised caregivers who have to care for loved ones with specific illnesses, for example, caregivers for elderly with dementia, caregivers of people with mental illness and parents of children with special needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that some of these specialised caregivers will qualify for tax reliefs, such as Handicapped Parent Relief or the Grandparent Care-giver Relief.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, tax reliefs are only meaningful for working Singaporeans with large enough incomes to pay taxes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many specialised caregivers either cannot work or work part-time due to the nature of the specialised caregiving.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also understand that some Government subsidies are available at the point of service, for example, for the Singapore Programme for Integrated Care for the Elderly (SPICE) and also the Foreign Domestic Worker (FDW) grant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We are a country with limited resources, and we cannot afford to be like some of the countries in the western world which spend a large proportion of their national budgets and gross domestic product (GDP) on welfare schemes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is, therefore, necessary for us to strike a right balance in how we allocate our resources for these schemes that we put in place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First is the philosophy that the less privileged should receive more.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The second issue, however, is much harder – how do we determine who the less privileged are, and should there be a scale to distinguish them and, hence, how much assistance they receive?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This issue undergirds the importance of means testing, which is the basis on which our resources for transfers are allocated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Over the years, Singapore has enacted a wide range of welfare schemes that seek to benefit many low-income families and they are targeted at the vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: These include system schemes such as Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS), ComCare, the Silver Support Scheme, the Post-Secondary Education Account (PSEA) for education bursaries, and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For example, in healthcare, the MediShield Life scheme, which provides medical coverage for all Singaporeans and Permanent Residents, tiers its premium subsidies solely based on home AV and monthly household income.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The MediSave Top-Up scheme also looks at the home AV.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For instance, the emphasis on AV is perhaps something of a misnomer in the context of means testing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As a result of this, a number of people who need assistance could well fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And let me elaborate a little on this point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There are families who live in private estates, but who may have little or no regular income to get by on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Many of them are likely to be elderly; they have inherited their homes or acquired it many years ago and have lived in this home all their lives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: They may live in a property which has good AV, but they are cash poor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But we tell them that because of their home AV, they will fail to qualify for many of the social schemes which they might need.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: To this group of people, AV is indeed something of a misnomer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is really no answer to tell these people that they should sell their home, their property, relocate and live off the remaining proceeds of the sale.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We would only be dislocating many of them from their homes; the environment they have grown comfortable with and this would directly, in my view, undermine efforts at fostering the social fabric within our communities we have strived so hard to build.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Another quibble I have with the present system is that the means test merely uses the home address on the National Registration Identity Card (NRIC).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It does not matter to the means tester whether the individual owns the property or not, whether he or she is renting or not, or could even be only temporarily living there on the goodwill of a friend or a family member.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The moment there is a private residential address, the means test criteria look immediately at the AV, regardless.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Because these factors, such as whether they actually own it or are just living there temporarily while they find their own feet and gain financial independence, do matter, and they might tell us a very different story of the financial sufficiency of the individual concerned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I, therefore, believe, Madam, that we need to look at refining the criteria for some of our social transfer schemes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Whilst current measures do provide a decent gauge of a household's or individuals' financial needs, I think more granulation needs to be undertaken.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, consider home ownership rather than just home residency.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Second, go beyond mere household type, in particular, for the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It has already been mentioned in this House that the current criteria need to be revised because indicators, such as household type alone, are not reflective of income and wealth, and I agree.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Additionally, these factors need to take into account needs-based wants, such as the existence of permanent and also severe illnesses, which are factors that are, more often than not, present among our elderly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Third, have a deeper inquiry into income status and also consider special cases where, despite having a good annual or per capita income, the family unit could be facing significant financial strains.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For example, where members of the family could be unemployed due to temporary sickness, disability, or where a family is headed by a lone parent of young children.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, some of these factors that I have mentioned have been borrowed from some of the factors that I have seen used by the UK government, in relation to how they qualify their citizens for support.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, with that, I urge this House and the Minister to consider reviewing the means so that the means tested criteria are fairer and they allow for a bigger span and better allocation of our resources so that our Budgets can be maximised and our resources directly applied specifically to those who need them more.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among some of the biggest compliance burdens that companies face is the necessity of computing detailed records of inputs and outputs to qualify for grants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have encountered business owners who complained of their grant applications being rejected multiple times due to submission of inadequate information.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sometimes, outputs are intangible and the applicant is unsure of how to put these into measurable amounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These could lead to significant losses when the applications fail to get approved in time for the deadline of that particular financial year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sometimes, businesses which cannot cope with the necessary administrative work will have to hire someone to handle the administrative work and that adds to significant compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On top of that, SMEs may overlook regulatory and compliance requirements, and this can lead to even higher costs to the business when it is subject to penalties for defaulting on payments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More outreach and handholding must be done to ensure that SMEs practise voluntary compliance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: SMEs should run through their business model with an appropriate professional, trained in legal matters to aid them in understanding and planning for regulatory and compliance requirements.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the key thrusts of the Smart Nation programme is to harness info communications technology (ICT) networks and data to support better living, create more opportunities and enable stronger communities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Networks of sensors and smart devices will enable better collection of data and the creation of user-specific solutions that will enable more targeted and efficient service delivery of Government services to citizens and businesses.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While the greater use of data and technology can increase the efficiency of service delivery, how do we maintain a human touch in the process, especially if there are outlier cases?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And how do we ensure that the needs of the elderly or the less Internet-savvy can continue to be met?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And while technology allows our communities to connect to one another more easily and intensely, how do we guard against domination of data share by vocal groups and continue to deliver solutions that are beneficial to the majority of our citizens and businesses?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yet, a number of Pioneer Generation Singaporeans do not have a computer at home or a handphone.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some are not computer literate, and residents with mobility needs can find it difficult to go to the nearest community centre or shared computer facility.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As we move towards a Smart Nation, we must ensure that we are a Smart Inclusive Nation, where no Singaporean is left behind because they lack a computer, lack computer knowledge or lack access to a shared computer facility.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our digital journey must empower all Singaporeans and not become a regressive situation where the less advantaged and those with disabilities are unable to access digital services.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I would like the Government and the Minister to also look into the plight of the middle-income earners, especially those with families.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: More often than not, they are sandwiched as they do not enjoy the benefits given to low-wage workers and neither do they have the high disposable income like those high up in the pyramid.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we all agree that the best security is job security and the best way to ensure employability is by staying relevant in the same industry through upskilling or in a different industry through reskilling.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The apprenticeship scheme should be age-blind or age-neutral, so that those inclined to take up the scheme with wage support assistance from the Government could benefit.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This would allow the middle-income earners to stand a chance or career surf.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will address three broad themes that were raised in the debate: first, how the Government can partner industry to facilitate innovation and growth through our procurement processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members spoke about support for innovative SMEs, co-creation of solutions and helping smaller firms access Government procurement opportunities; second, principles underlying our procurement approach; and third, improving the ease of doing business and reducing compliance burdens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will address the other cuts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We share Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Miss Cheryl Chan's views that Government agencies should be open to developing innovative solutions together with the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The world today is becoming increasingly complex and the multi-faceted issues we face require us to work in partnership with one another, each playing our part.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And this is the spirit of partnership underlying this year's Budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Government agencies are crowdsourcing ideas more, and involving communities and businesses in problem solving through hackathons and innovation challenges where individuals and firms can participate in developing and co-creating innovative solutions to challenges faced by businesses or the society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, in the Infocomm Development Authority of Singapore’s (IDA) Hackathon@SG last year, Goji, the winning team, developed a data visualisation tool which allows corporate and financial data from the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) to be easily and quickly viewed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This can potentially be developed further for credit risk analysis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA is working with the team to explore how we can implement the idea.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Another example is the recently deployed Volunteer Broadcast System mobile app for Food from the Heart.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many are familiar with Food from the Heart, a non-profit organisation whose volunteers collect unsold bread from bakeries and hotels daily and deliver it to welfare organisations and self-collection centres within the heartlands for distribution to beneficiaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Previously, volunteers had to call in to the coordinating centre to plan their delivery routes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The centre staff had to manually search and suggest delivery routes for the volunteers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To get replacement volunteers, the centre had to call volunteers individually, a manually intensive task.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At a GeoHackathon event organised by the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), one of the winning ideas was an app that used SLA's geospatial data to update the organisation and its volunteers on real-time collection and delivery information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With the app, volunteers can quickly identify which collection or distribution point has not been visited and select their routes, without having to call the centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What used to take 30 minutes to find a volunteer replacement is now just a "click away" and this has significantly improved productivity for both the centre and the volunteers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa will be pleased to know that as we promote the generation of new ideas, we also seek to adopt more flexible procurement processes, where practicable, to facilitate the adoption of innovative solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This approach allows vendors to propose innovative solutions to develop prototypes and potentially be awarded the contract subsequently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A good example is IDA and the Sentosa Development Corporation's (SDC) recent Integrated Guest Experience Innovation Challenge, an open invitation for participants to develop ideas to enhance guest experience for visitors to Sentosa.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Proposed ideas included innovative solutions involving data analytics, wearable devices, virtual assistants and augmented reality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SDC is currently exploring the possibility of inviting the shortlisted participants to develop their prototypes for implementation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This would enable tenderers to consider using technology and innovative deployment of their staff to support our efforts to raise productivity and wages in these sectors, a point made by Mr Zainal Sapari in his Budget Debate speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This alternative procurement approach will require Government agencies to change the way they call and evaluate tenders and how they monitor service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will also require changes by service providers in the way they respond to tenders and provide their services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will involve some effort, but we believe that this is a move in the right direction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa also asked about the PPCIP initiative and suggested that it be boosted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The rocks had little value in themselves but, with this initiative, the rocks have acquired a new value, and the initiative has potential to be implemented across other new roads in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is an illustration of how a partnership between the public and private sectors can create value for our enterprises while meeting public needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, we are reviewing the initiative to see how it can be more effective in public-private co-innovation, alongside other existing efforts to promote collaboration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This share of the total number of Government contracts is significantly higher than in other countries, such as the UK.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our SMEs have successfully tendered not just for smaller projects, but also for more sizeable ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We would encourage more SMEs to participate in Government procurement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Those who need information on how to go about doing so can refer to the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING Singapore) and MOF websites.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SMEs are also encouraged to attend the engagement sessions organised by industry associations and the Government to better understand Government procurement processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, earlier this year, the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) organised a Government Procurement Fair for SMEs, where various Government agencies, including MOF, participated to clarify the Government's procurement practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SBF is also developing a Best Practice Guide to help SMEs better understand Government procurement principles and processes and how to bid for Government contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Another simple but useful thing which SMEs can do to improve their access to Government procurement opportunities is just register for a Government Electronic Business (GeBIZ) account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If you are registered on GeBIZ, you will automatically receive alerts on new procurement opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The system also allows businesses to save their business information, making it easier for them to submit bids.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Registration is straightforward and can be done online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Best of all, registration of the first GeBIZ account is free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To help suppliers find and participate in Government procurement opportunities, we revamped the Government procurement portal GeBIZ in January this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The revamped portal has a more user-friendly interface which was developed following extensive consultations with businesses that use the portal and has received much positive feedback from existing suppliers and new users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to work with the industry associations to improve outreach and education to SMEs in this area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also recognise that SMEs without a track record may find it challenging to win tenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are open to helping SMEs with innovative ideas and quality products to compete and establish their track record.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: An example of how we do this is the Accreditation@IDA programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Set up in 2014, this programme helps promising Singapore-based technology startups to establish their track record to have a better chance at securing Government and private sector projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The accreditation programme evaluates and accredits companies to give potential buyers the assurance of their quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IDA also partners companies in their development process by providing advice and recommendations to strengthen their product, improve financial management, and better manage intellectual property.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We expect more to be accredited in due course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have also revised our Government procurement rules, within the parameters of our international trade agreements, to make it easier for Government agencies to procure innovative solutions from these companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They will be considered first when agencies seek to buy technology services or products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Subject to obligations under international trade agreements, we are open to working with suitable industry partners to recognise promising startups in other sectors so that they can compete favourably for contracts and build up their track record.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In his Budget debate speech, Mr Zainal Sapari suggested using Government procurement practices to achieve certain objectives, such as raising wages for low-income workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chen Show Mao also talked about price escalation clauses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I thought it would be helpful to clarify the Government's approach on this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The objective of public tenders is to procure goods and services required for the delivery of public services in a fair and transparent manner and, given that we are spending public monies, to obtain value-for-money in our procurement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Value-for-money does not mean always and only going for the lowest price.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Agencies also consider quality factors in their evaluation as this has a bearing on value and these are spelt out in the tender documents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where Government intervention is required to meet certain policy objectives, we generally do this through targeted measures rather than through conditions of procurement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This avoids mixing multiple objectives into the Government procurement process which could result in distorted outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, for example, to help social enterprises, which Miss Cheryl Chan spoke about, the Singapore Centre for Social Enterprise, also known as raiSE, was set up to provide support in areas, such as funding, business advisory and training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We believe that this is a better approach to helping social enterprises stay viable rather than to artificially set aside Government contracts to sustain them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, in very specific instances where the evidence suggests that Government procurement practices can make a substantial difference, we will take the appropriate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, we have our effort to support the Progressive Wage Model in the cleaning, security and landscape sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, in other sectors where procurement policy is not a suitable or appropriate means of impacting wages, we have other ways to assist, such as through the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), which has been enhanced in this Budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari also spoke about unfair contracts and options to extend.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Options to extend contracts are a common practice internationally and in the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The benefit of an option to extend is that it enables a longer-term relationship with the supplier if the supplier has provided good quality service and demonstrates the ability to continue to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The extension also means continued employment of the suppliers' employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It could operate unfairly, however, if the extension does not allow for any increase in contract price in subsequent years to take into account wage increments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This can be avoided if price increases upon extension are factored in from the outset.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our practice is to ask Government agencies to remind tenderers of multi-year contracts to factor in wage increments for their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also explicitly allow tenderers to present their price bid on a year-by-year basis, so as to factor in annual wage increments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chen Show Mao spoke about encouraging the increased use of price escalation clauses in Government contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are open to this in the appropriate situations and where it is right to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, in standard clauses for construction contracts, we do explicitly allow for material price fluctuations based on material price indices which are published by the Building and Construction Authority (BCA), and that is based on objective indices which are published independently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What I would suggest in this case, really, is for the tenderers to propose this if they feel that either the price of the materials or anything that forms part of their costs, is something which would be subject to fluctuation and needs to have some sort of price escalation in years to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is something that they should raise with the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Of course, we welcome feedback as we learn from them as well as the practices in other countries and the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will also continue to raise the capabilities of our procurement officers and community in the public sector, so that they can handle Government procurement well and ensure that public monies are spent prudently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked what can be done to reduce the compliance burden and facilitate the ease of doing business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As we press on to transform our industries, we will continue to review our regulations to facilitate doing business in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include exempting small companies from statutory audits and allowing public companies to issue non-voting or multiple vote shares.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF and ACRA are reviewing other corporate regulations to facilitate business, including: (a) requirements on the use of common company seals; (b) the holding of annual general meetings (AGMs); and (c) the filing of annual returns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Details of the proposed changes will be announced during MOF's public consultation on the regulations later this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to work closely with businesses to avoid unnecessary burdens on businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Sun Xueling highlighted the need to ensure that our licensing requirements remain conducive for promising new technology and business models in her Budget debate speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Pro-Enterprise Panel, comprising business leaders and senior public officers, was set up in 2000 as an internal advocate for businesses within the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Panel works closely with public agencies to provide timely, effective and practical solutions to address the regulatory concerns that businesses face, including those in new technology areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Saktiandi also highlighted that some companies might inadvertently overlook regulatory and compliance requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On our part, we try to reduce the likelihood of default.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where possible, our agencies facilitate compliance by sending reminders ahead of statutory deadlines, such as for AGMs and filing of annual returns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA has also partnered other Government agencies, such as the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), the CPF Board and SPRING Singapore, to organise information sessions on statutory obligations for new and aspiring business owners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Saktiandi also commented on difficulties faced by SMEs in applying for business grants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is a question of achieving the right balance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In administering grant schemes, the Government is accountable for the money spent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We, therefore, require information to monitor the output of the support we give to businesses to ensure that the money is used for the proper purpose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, we recognise that applications for grants should not be unduly burdensome and a deterrent instead of an encouragement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As such, we constantly review the appropriate level of documentation and information that is required for grant applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Advancements in ICT have raised public expectations of Government service delivery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: On the Government's part, we have taken efforts to transform service delivery and bring about more convenience for the public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There is room for improvement and the Public Service will continue to do so, amidst tighter constraints on public sector manpower growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Public Service has embarked on a multi-year transformation journey into a Digital Government, with citizens at the heart of it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will redesign online services and underlying processes to make them simpler to use and easier to access, including providing more services on mobile devices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some agencies, such as the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), have already begun to do this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: MOM has made online foreign domestic worker (FDW) permit renewals much easier for employers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There has also been a 40% reduction in call centre enquiries related to renewals over the same period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Renewed permits are also directly couriered to employers, increasing the convenience of self-renewal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We want more high-volume Government services to be similarly redesigned to be intuitive for users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: An idea we are pursuing is to integrate and digitise key services around important milestones in life for individuals and businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will facilitate more data sharing to make it easier for businesses and citizens to transact with the Government and deliver more targeted and effective services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For businesses, the National Trade Platform (NTP) will significantly improve digital connectivity across businesses in the logistics and trade finance sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As announced by the Minister for Finance in his Budget speech, NTP will facilitate data sharing for both business-to-business and business-to-Government transactions to help SMEs cut costs and streamline processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the firm level, businesses will be able to digitise their documents or information to support data sharing, with the help of software tools or applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Electronic data shared among all parties in the supply chain will allow them to have sight of information related to their cargoes and better manage their resources accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the industry level, by connecting importers, exporters, logistics service providers, NTP will enable each party to establish linkages with multiple partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Such data sharing on this Government-owned platform could yield further collaborations across partners in terms of resource sharing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There may also be downstream benefits for associated sectors, such as trade financing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For instance, financial institutions could use the data transmitted to expedite trade finance operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: NTP will be designed as an open innovation platform which businesses can tap on to develop new applications that support evolving business needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As we embark on this, we welcome industries and businesses to come forward with ideas and partner us to create solutions that are relevant for the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The National Electronic Health Records (NEHR) project was rolled out by the Ministry of Health (MOH) in 2012 to allow participating healthcare institutions to access the same set of patient records for seamless healthcare delivery across the national healthcare network.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With NEHR, patients no longer need to worry about being brought to the nearest public hospital that is different from the one they regularly visit, as all public hospitals will have access to the same set of medical history.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Today, the secure use of data by authorised clinicians and healthcare professionals supports more accurate diagnosis, better treatment and patient-centric integrated care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It also helps to reduce the cost for patients as duplicated tests and referrals can be avoided.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Compared to a year earlier, there has been a significant increase of 63% in users and over three times the number of searches.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan asked whether digitalisation could inadvertently result in a lack of clarity over ownership of issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We wish to assure Members that technology remains an enabler and will not displace or diffuse responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In fact, technology allows for greater accountability as requests by citizens could be traced and tagged to specific agencies for resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We agree there is a need to debunk the impression that digitalisation will create more work and lower efficiency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our Digital Government strategy aims to enhance productivity by actively using data and technology not just for service delivery, but also to change the way we work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This twin focus will be vital for the public sector to function more efficiently and respond more quickly to citizens' service needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: By 2020, at least six agencies will digitise the majority of their records and processes for higher productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They are the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA), IRAS, MOM, VITAL, the Supreme Court and the State Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Citizens will benefit from easier access to Government information and e-services from home or on the go.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some of these efforts will also reduce the need for repetitive submission of information to agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For instance, ICA will digitise records and implement an enterprise-wide case and content management system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is expected to lead to an overall productivity gain through integrated processes and better case management that will see a reduction in the need for duplicate data entry when a case is routed from one unit to another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If required, users of ICA's services will only need to submit supporting documents once, rather than resubmitting each time they apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Digitalisation will also reduce backend paper processing and result in better auditing, security and data protection processes within organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: VITAL, the Government's shared services department under MOF, has begun integrating human resources (HR), payroll and claims processes for civil servants while concurrently using information technology (IT) systems to reduce paperwork, capture and retain information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This will facilitate better document management, thus making it easier to carry out audits and reduce paper handling in the process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are also improving arrangements and facilitating e-payments in order to reap similar benefits and greater convenience for users of Government services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Miss Cheryl Chan have pointed out that there will be some who will have difficulties accessing digital services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Indeed, even as we make transacting digitally a way of life, we must not forget that there may be some Singaporeans who may not be comfortable with or know how to use digital services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Since 2005, we have built up a network of 26 Citizen Connect Centres (CCCs) islandwide for those who do not have computers or Internet connection and those who need help to use Government e-services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Trained staff are on hand at CCCs to assist and teach users to access Government services online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The goal for CCCs is to teach users to transact online independently, so that they can access Government services from the comfort of their own homes in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But even if they find it hard to learn, they will still be helped at the CCCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: CCC+s will complement the existing suite of initiatives by the Ministry of Communications and Information and IDA for the elderly, persons with disabilities, and low-income households to help them get online and stay online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Ms Sun Xueling also asked how we can maintain a human touch amidst more digitalisation within the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even as we go digital, the Government will continue to provide face-to-face services, where necessary, for example, in reaching out to less connected groups like the elderly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As Dr Tan Wu Meng pointed out, there are some Pioneer Generation residents with mobility needs who may find it difficult to access shared terminals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Pioneer Generation Ambassadors (PGAs) serve as one key touch point to convey policy information, such as the Pioneer Generation Package and MediShield Life, to our Pioneers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Minister for Finance spoke about the Community Network for Seniors pilot led by MOH.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will continue to strengthen coordination among Government agencies, VWOs and local volunteers, and build strong community networks to provide support and engage the elderly within the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are also continuing with the face-to-face approach when gathering feedback.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH), the Government feedback unit, continues to retain face-to-face engagement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For example, for Budget 2016, it has held 12 such engagements so far, where close to 3,800 Singaporeans from all walks of life have participated and given their views.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Ms Thanaletchimi's points on the middle class, as well as apprenticeship, were largely addressed in the Minister for Finance's round-up speech and also at the MOM's Committee of Supply (COS) debate last week and, in the interest of time, I will not repeat those points here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked if refundable income tax credits could be provided for specialised caregivers of dependants with special needs, including autism and dementia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In essence, the Member is asking if direct cash grants can be provided for caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We recognise that caregivers play an important role, which can be very demanding and challenging, and we should support them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our approach is to focus on directly subsidising services required by people with special needs, thereby defraying the costs borne by their families and caregivers, rather than by providing cash allowances to people for looking after their family members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This has been our consistent approach, as reflected in previous replies on this subject by office holders overseeing health, social support and ageing policies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Caregivers who work can tap on subsidised centre-based care services when they are working, such as Special Student Care Centres for students, and dementia day care and home help services for seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will continue to expand the capacity of these services, especially as our population ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They also benefit from tax reliefs, such as the handicapped parent relief and the handicapped child relief, if applicable, which reduce the tax they have to pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Caregivers can also benefit from a training grant to equip themselves with the necessary skills to care for their loved ones, and self-care skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are also strengthening respite care to enable caregivers to take a much-needed break at times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Should caregivers require additional assistance beyond what is already available, we have existing social safety nets to help them when required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will continue to explore further ways to help persons with special needs and dementia, as well as their caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development has recently set up a committee to look into the next Enabling Masterplan and it will be studying various initiatives to support persons with disabilities, and their caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: MOH will speak more about enhancing support for those with dementia as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Mr Edwin Tong asked about reviewing means-testing for our social schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I am glad that the Member supports our principle of having a progressive system of taxes and benefits, where lower- and middle-income households pay a smaller share of taxes and receive a larger share of benefits, while higher-income households pay a larger share of taxes and receive a smaller share of benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I am also glad that the Member recognises the importance of means testing so that benefits can be provided in a targeted manner to those who need help more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Very importantly, the Member has also affirmed that with limited resources, we have to be careful with spending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Indeed, we have a responsibility to manage our fiscal burden prudently and to be fair to future generations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Member has suggested other needs-based factors to refine the qualifying criteria for schemes, in particular, to overcome the perceived drawbacks of using the Annual Value (AV) of the property.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I also find myself frequently thinking about the points he has raised as I look after both Housing and Development Board (HDB) residents and private estate residents in my role as a Member of Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The challenge in determining means-testing criteria for social support schemes is deciding on relevant measures that are clear, reasonable and practical to implement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Typically, this involves measures of income and wealth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There are, of course, trade-offs with each criterion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If we take current income, we may not, as the Member has pointed out, have a longer-term picture of the families' financial means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But if we take income over a few years, as the Member has suggested, we might also not be as responsive to recent deterioration in the financial situation of a household.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: AV is frequently used as a measure of wealth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Furthermore, because the data does not need to be separately collected, using AV allows benefits to be delivered automatically to recipients without them having to apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is an important consideration for schemes like the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Voucher, and indeed for better Government service delivery overall.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Member can be assured that appeals by those who are in need and in exceptional circumstances will be carefully considered on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This includes, for instance, appeals from those who are not related to the owners of the homes they live in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Member suggested that we consider incorporating other needs-based eligibility factors used in the UK's Income Support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We note that this scheme is a targeted one based on application, and also requires other criteria, such as the amount of personal savings the individual and his spouse have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We do have schemes, such as the ComCare Short- to Medium-Term Assistance, that take into account the unique needs of each family that applies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I would also like to share that such targeted schemes form only a small part of the total amount of benefits that Singaporeans, including private property dwellers, receive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Broad-based schemes that involve less or no targeting include (a) healthcare subsidies, (b) education subsidies for primary education to tertiary education, (c) training subsidies like the SkillsFuture credit, (d) Marriage and Parenthood Package, (e) lower Foreign Domestic Worker levies for those with young children or the elderly, and (f) the Senior Citizen Transport Concession.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have a little bit of time for clarifications.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Could the Senior Minister of State update us further on what she means by upgrading of equipment and redesigning of online interfaces?

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will also ensure that CCC officers are well-trained to provide assistance to the visitors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I actually suggested to move away from the preceding year system to a current year system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I was wondering whether MOF can share whether they are looking into it or are there any plans, going forward, to look into it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: One of the reasons why I raised that was because it could help some of the retrenched or some of the professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) going forward, given that it will also act as an automatic stabiliser for the economic system as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I hope MOF can shed some light on my suggestion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think what we can say, Mdm Chairman, is that we have taken note of the suggestion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will look into it, and in due course, if there is anything to be done further on it, of course, we will let the public know.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: We are into the new financial year (FY) 2016.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Are there any Government programmes or functions of the Government which are affected because of the later than usual COS?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in this case, as Parliament opened at the beginning of the calendar year in January, we had a very heavy Parliamentary schedule, and so, the Government's Budget was presented on 24 March 2016, taking into account the President's Address and the debate on the proposed policies as well as programmes of the Government in January.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Supply Bill 2016 can, therefore, only be passed by Parliament and enacted after the start of our financial year and, under the Order Paper, Parliament is currently scheduled to vote on the Bill after the end of COS on 14 April 2016.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Once passed, the Bill would be submitted to the President for assent before it can be enacted as the Supply Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think, really, Mr Liang Eng Hwa's question pertains to that period after the end of the preceding financial year on 31 March to the time the Supply Bill is passed and how we are funded for that period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under Article 148B (4) of the Constitution, the Finance Minister, with the Cabinet's approval, can authorise spending from various Government funds to keep public services running until the Supply Bills are passed into law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, the amount that is spent must not exceed one quarter of the total sum approved for the particular service in the past year's Budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in this case, the Government is able to continue its operations as per normal as the Finance Minister has, with the prior approval of the Cabinet, authorised interim expenditure pending the Supply Bill becoming law under Article 148B (4) of the Constitution and we are, therefore, funded for this period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This has been done before, in 2002 when, likewise, the new Parliament opened on 25 March 2002 and Budget Day was on 3 May 2002, thus pushing back the Parliamentary calendar and requiring interim funding under Article 148B (4) of the Constitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: One of the chief problems faced by specialised caregivers is their own retirement adequacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Government assistance and direct subsidies, at the point of service, help them for the immediate needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But many of them are themselves well advanced in age after the end of care and will not do well in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: My question is: how is the Government looking into enhancing the retirement adequacy of this group in the long run?

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Government is concerned about the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans who may not have had the opportunity to work or to build up their savings either in cash or in their CPF.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: That includes, but is not limited to caregivers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There are also various assistance schemes which we have mentioned broadly, which are meant to supplement either the incomes of those who are in greater need or to help them cope with living expenses.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: And in keeping with tradition, we have kept the MOF COS short and sweet.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Once again, congratulations to Minister Heng Swee Keat and the MOF team for the truly transformational Budget and also thanks to Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah and Senior Minister of State Sim Ann for their replies, notwithstanding the short time that they have.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: So, with that, Madam, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
